title: The Bell of the Undercroft
premise: Gideon Blackwood, a pest controller who prides herself on never believing in anything, is hired to clear the undercroft of Harrowmere House, where something leaves fingerprints on the inside of sealed doors. When she plays back her client's sleep recordings, a second voice answers the questions no one asked aloud — and it knows her name. To survive, Gideon must learn the bell-song's final verse from the thing below without ever singing along, because the last heir who sang it became the house. In the end she silences the bell by taking its toll into her own body, walking out of Harrowmere alive but forever humming a tune she refuses to finish.
about_author: Odile Quintana is a former archivist of ecclesiastical records who spent a decade cataloguing parish bells and their inscriptions before turning to fiction. She writes horror rooted in old buildings, oral tradition, and the quiet violence of inheritance.

chapters.title: The Call-Out Fee
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. A routine vermin contract at derelict Harrowmere House comes with an absurd clause: work stops at dusk. Gideon takes the job for the money, mocking the superstitious caretaker. Emotional beat: dry skepticism establishing her armor of disbelief.

chapters.title: Fingerprints on the Inside
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. In the undercroft she finds greasy handprints pressed against the inside of a bricked-up door — small, adult-sized, too many joints per finger. She photographs them and tells herself it's a prank. Beat: first crack in her certainty, masked as professional irritation.

chapters.title: The Client Who Sleeps Standing Up
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Her employer, Miss Vane, last of the Harrowmere line, hires her to stay overnight and record the house's sounds. Vane sleeps in a chair by the bell rope, upright, hands folded. Beat: unease dressed as eccentric wealth; the inheritance theme surfaces.

chapters.title: Static and a Second Voice
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Reviewing the night's recordings, Gideon hears Vane murmur questions in her sleep — and a second voice, wet and patient, answering each one. The last answer is Gideon's own name. Beat: dread arrives through evidence, the skeptic's own medium turned against her.

chapters.title: Questions No One Asked
chapters.summary: Vane's POV. Vane explains the family bargain: the bell in the undercroft rings once a generation, and a Harrowmere must teach it a new verse or it teaches itself. She has been feeding it questions for years to keep it docile. Beat: confession as burden; power inherited like debt.

chapters.title: The Undercroft Bell
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Gideon breaks through the bricked door and finds a bronze bell with no clapper, warm to the touch, ringed by handprints centuries deep. It hums when she breathes near it. Beat: awe curdling into violation; the house notices her.

chapters.title: What the Caretaker Knew
chapters.summary: Caretaker Moss's POV. Old Moss recounts the 1911 ringing, when his grandmother sang along and was found hollowed, still smiling. He warns Gideon: never hum what you hear. Beat: folklore as survival manual; foreshadowing the verse rule.

chapters.title: Overnight Retainer
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Contractually bound to stay, Gideon rigs sensors and sleeps in her van. At 3 a.m. every sensor trips at once, and her own recorder captures her voice asking questions she doesn't remember asking. Beat: loss of ownership over self; rising dread.

chapters.title: The Verse Fragment
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Transcribing the recordings, she isolates three lines of a song in the second voice's register. Written down, they won't leave her head; she catches herself tapping their rhythm. Beat: contamination begins; knowledge as infection.

chapters.title: Miss Vane's Ledger
chapters.summary: Vane's POV. Vane shows Gideon the family ledger: every heir's entry ends mid-sentence except those who 'paid the toll.' Vane intends Gideon to be this generation's payment — the contract was a summons. Betrayal beat: the price of survival is someone else.

chapters.title: Run or Ring
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Gideon tries to walk out; the drive loops back to Harrowmere no matter which road she takes. Her phone plays the fragment in her own voice while off. Beat: trap closes; panic managed through competence.

chapters.title: Moss's Bargain
chapters.summary: Moss's POV. Moss reveals the caretakers' side-deal: they serve the bell in exchange for their families' safety, and he can buy Gideon one night's grace if she gives it something true. She gives it her mother's lullaby. Beat: sacrifice as currency; complicity.

chapters.title: One Night's Grace
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. The grace holds until dawn, during which Gideon researches the bell's casting: it was poured with the ashes of the first Harrowmere heir who refused to sing. The fourth verse exists only in that heir's line — Vane's line. Beat: hope with a hook; plan forms.

chapters.title: The Hollow Choir
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Descending again, Gideon finds the previous 'pests' — generations of hired hands, preserved, mouths open, standing in a ring around the bell. They turn toward her light in unison. Beat: horror climax of imagery; the cost of every past survivor made visible.

chapters.title: Vane Sings
chapters.summary: Vane's POV. Cornered by the bell's impatience, Vane attempts the fourth verse herself, believing bloodright will protect her. She sings along — and begins to come apart into harmony, her voice splitting into the choir. Beat: power corrupts its inheritor; hubris punished.

chapters.title: What the Bell Wants
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. The bell speaks plainly through the choir: it doesn't want worship, it wants completion — a verse sung by someone who chooses it freely. Choice, not blood, is the toll. Beat: the rules invert; agency becomes both danger and weapon.

chapters.title: Learning Without Singing
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Gideon negotiates: she will learn the fourth verse note by note, writing it, signing it, never voicing it. Each line learned costs her a memory — her father's face goes first. Beat: mounting personal price; grief as tuition.

chapters.title: The Last Verse
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. The final line requires the singer to name what they'd become to survive. Gideon writes the truth — that she'd let the whole choir stay hollow if it meant walking out — and the bell accepts the honesty itself as the verse. Beat: dark catharsis; survival's ugly arithmetic confessed.

chapters.title: Toll
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Climax. The bell demands its payment in person. Gideon strikes it once with the old clapper she's kept hidden, pouring the written verse into the strike. The bell cracks; the choir exhales at last and collapses into dust. Beat: violent, costly resolution of the central bargain.

chapters.title: Aftermath at Harrowmere
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Dawn. Vane survives, emptied of the family gift, weeping over a ledger now full of finished sentences. Moss burns his caretaker's keys. Gideon invoices for pest removal, completed. Beat: exhausted relief; the mundane reclaiming ground.

chapters.title: Humming
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Weeks later, Gideon notices she hums constantly — a tune she never finishes, cutting off before the last note every time. Doctors find nothing. She starts carrying earplugs and avoiding churches. Beat: lingering dread; survival's residue.

chapters.title: The Next Call-Out
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. A new client calls about fingerprints on the inside of a cellar door two counties away. Gideon says no — then hears herself humming the fourth verse, complete, for the first time. She picks up the keys. Beat: cyclical ending; inheritance passed whether or not she consents.
